title: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
text:
Even though decades have passed, part of me feels I should not be telling this story. Not because it isn’t true, but because telling makes it real. And the reality is very hard to bear.
I was a young child at home in Whitechapel, east London, when my mother came into my bedroom, which was next to my parents’, and told me that my father had raped her. He had gone off to work and I was too young to fully understand what the words meant – perhaps seven or eight – and I remember being angry with her for upsetting life again, as she had done before, when she suddenly came to me at the top of the stairs and told me that they would “have to part” and that would mean taking me away with her.
I couldn’t understand why life couldn’t just be nice in our house, a brick terrace with a handsome exterior, shabby inside and a crack through the stone of the front steps. Down in the dark basement and back yard, my mother had painted spectacular murals of exotic jungles and savannah filled with giraffes, elephants, leopards, tigers, hummingbirds, eagles and tree frogs.
I had my books and teddies and crafting station, and in photos it looks like I was filled with my mother’s joy and hope and creativity and happiness. But even if I didn’t have words for it at the time, my body did. I was tense from lack of sleep and bit my nails so relentlessly that my fingers are still bent. I couldn’t bear to be separated from my mother, following her around the house and refusing even to be left at nursery.
The love for my father that I felt when he told me scary stories, took me down to Brick Lane market, rescued old bikes from the canal, or lifted me up so that I could “walk on the ceiling” in the kitchen began to morph into something deeply uncomfortable, a feeling of the frightening tension between how you want things to be and how they have turned out. This came back to me with the trial of Russell Brand. Both he and my father did terrible things when no one was watching – and both were celebrated by the media. Looking back now, if I could have any wish granted, I’d see my father jailed for life.
Or maybe I’d just tell my mother to run and never look back. But it’s too late for that. She died in 2000, when I was 24, but in effect the death came much earlier.
It was around 1973 when Sally Hill, a bright 23-year-old final year student at Camberwell art school in London, first met my father, Brian, who was 47 and a friend of a member of staff. The younger brother of the famous writer, Brendan Behan, he was just starting work as a lecturer in media and general studies at the London College of Printing, having recently graduated from the University of Sussex and done a teacher training course. Prior to meeting my father, my mother had been dating a much younger man called Terry Scott, a boxer who unfortunately also knew my father and his first family, who were living on a houseboat in Shoreham in West Sussex. Terry took Sally down to visit and it wasn’t long before my mother was living on the boat too.
Having been discharged from the Irish army, my father had originally arrived in England with nothing and worked on building sites, quickly marrying his first wife, the daughter of his Communist landlord, when she was 16 and he was 24. After having three daughters with her, he had transitioned out of trade unionism and into teaching, despite a criminal record that included a six-week spell in prison for using threatening behaviour and insulting words to police during a strike.
According to one of his friends, he was unhappy before he met my mother and seemed markedly better afterwards. While he may have thought he loved my mother, calling her “the most beautiful woman I’ve ever seen”, it didn’t take long for his fanatically deep-seated sense of resentment to set in, especially once she started to argue with him about his unreasonable demands and lack of support. He claimed to hate traditional family structures, yet seemed to see her as his possession, to the extent that she soon found herself being held responsible for his erratic moods or anything that went wrong. Any challenge would result in a barrage of verbal, psychological and physical abuse.
This was not and would never be a fair or mutual relationship. She was not allowed to work because he was afraid she’d meet someone else, and despite her huge talent for painting, drawing and sculpture, these activities began to dwindle as his behaviour escalated after my birth in 1976.
My mother’s skills were perceived as a threat, and instead of celebrating her, my father rarely mentioned her, except to his close friends. Although he earned a good salary and we benefited from cheap lodging thanks to my maternal grandmother, who got the house through her job in the NHS, he got her to claim benefits as a “single mother”. Then he used this against her by threatening to report her if he needed to get his way.
My mother never had a bank account, and later, when we moved to Brighton, my father would list her in his tally of weekly spending, giving her cash and then berating her for spending too much on cigarettes. On her death certificate he registered her occupation as “Housewife – Wife of Brian Desmond Behan Playwright”.
In 1979, he published his first, deeply unpleasant, novel Time to Go, an unsuccessful book about a violent, misogynistic man named O’Brien who feels trapped by marriage and resolves to go after a young woman named Jeannie. O’Brien woos her with lies, “love bombing” her (“Say I can see you or I’ll die. I mean it, I will die”), while concealing his “growing contempt” for women in general. But, of course, he wants their bodies: “He felt he would do anything from rape, sodomy, exposure, child molestation, lies, anything to get a feel of another woman.”
Describing himself as “the most jealous and insecure man on earth”, O’Brien goes on: “Many of their rows were the result of his nasty mind calculating times of outings, times of coming in at night, where she had been and whom she had seen. His secret desire to lock her up was just part of his desire to dominate her.”
Everything I have come to know about my father tells me this was a thinly veiled account of his own life and attitudes. My mother may have come to the same conclusion, but by the time he exposed himself in print, she was pregnant with my brother and her fate was sealed. Although she appeared strong to most people outside the family, the ambitious, happy-go-lucky free spirit went into retreat. In its place came a woman who created a tough front to push through the days, but behind it she was withdrawn, sad, confused and increasingly depressed, using alcohol to numb herself.
Meanwhile, my father was using the standard tactics of a skilled perpetrator, undermining her sense of self to the point that she questioned her own reality. He would tell her that things didn’t happen when they did, that she was exaggerating, or, when things really escalated, that no one would believe her because he had friends in the media and she was nothing, would never be anything.
As well as a gifted artist who taught me painting, screen printing, lino cutting, pottery, marbling, mask-making and candle making, Sally was a fantastic vegetarian cook, and decades ahead of her time in her understanding of the environment, health and educational theory. And she was, of course, a wonderful mother. Yet he was the one with the talent, he told her.
At some point, we got used to the dichotomy of a rich life filled with creativity and its horrible, almost unreal contrast. What is most devastating about domestic abusers is that they expertly tread the line of plausible deniability, so my father always had an excuse or “provocation” for his misdeeds. And since the bad was mixed with good, there was always the hope that next time would be different.
Early in their relationship, my father leveraged my mother’s compassion and kindness by telling her exaggerated stories about his abusive childhood, which he would bring up again after each beating, telling her he was sorry and that he loved her. The entire time I was growing up, he claimed to have been institutionalised in Artane, an industrial school in Dublin, for six years from the age of 10, after stealing money from a neighbour’s gas meter. In fact, according to official records, it was one year and seven months, and from the age of 13.
These industrial schools were mostly run by Catholic orders for the Irish state for supposedly “difficult” but often simply poor children, and mixed education with manual work. They were notorious for their brutality, and as the only one in the family to be sent to such a school, my father was set up for a life of grievance. But whatever sense of disadvantage he felt, he did his best to encourage it in others.
He homed in on the fact that my mother had never been told who her father was, and stoked her anxiety about it, at the same time as poisoning her relationships with my grandmother, Edna, and with my mother’s friends. Sally and Mick Arnup. They were renowned artists, who had taught my mother and lamented her ever meeting my father, since it meant the end of her career and they “never saw her again”, though they talked about her regularly for years.
Edna, with whom we lived until 1989, when we moved to Brighton, worked nights running the nurses’ home at the nearby London hospital. What none of us knew at the time, was that prior to my mother’s birth, she had abandoned a baby she could not afford to keep and been prosecuted, leaving her with both a conviction she was desperate to hide and public judgment around what she had done. She refused to name the baby’s father, or to ask for support, probably because he was married.
All of this only emerged after my mother’s death, when that baby – now a middle-aged man called Mike, living in Birmingham – got in touch. I would later find out that, including Sally and Mike, Edna, who died in 2013, had four children by four men.
I recall seeing Edna’s body on the floor during one violent episode. Her presence in the house must have had some protective effect, yet we were still living with her when my mother “fell” on the stairs and her face went through a window pane. I remember seeing her hair and blood on the broken glass the next morning and being very disturbed that she was apparently refusing to go to hospital.
The traumas of daily life, and the stress of keeping quiet about them, resulted in my mother’s multiple mental breakdowns (“I just can’t keep pretending,” she said) and failed attempts to escape. In 1988, weeks after marrying my father for perceived financial security, but then perhaps realising he was not going to change, my mother was sectioned at St Clement’s psychiatric hospital in Bow. Here, not only were signs of domestic abuse minimised and misunderstood, but she was subjected to forced medication and threatened with electroconvulsive therapy. She also said she endured further sexual assault on the mixed ward full of very disturbed people.
All this time, my father did his own thing, sought sympathy for what he had to “put up with” and took her on drinking binges whenever she got out, although at times her medication left her drooling and stupefied. Yet it was never about her, or us, anyway. His life revolved around him, with my mother’s purpose just to make his life better and easier. And, after a while, to let him indulge his sadistic side whenever he wanted. He would call her a “silly bitch”, a “fool”, and occasionally a “prostitute” – then that he “didn’t mean it”, or more usually, that she had “provoked” him. Eventually she started to believe it.
He could appear charming and brilliant, which made it hard for anyone, even sometimes us, to believe what a monster he could be. My mother was afraid of losing her children if she took action against him, especially when her mental health was brought into it. She told me several times that no one would believe her. Yet by the time I was a teenager and we were living in Brighton, I had started begging her to leave, and taking her to the police station – all to no avail.
I will never forget the time I challenged my father in our small living room after he had beaten her. “You shock me, Brian,” I told him (we called our parents by their first names), hoping that if I spoke loudly and authoritatively enough he would find some respect for me, if not for her. He just looked at me and smiled ghoulishly and said: “Good. I’m glad.”
When she died, aged 50 on Christmas Day 2000, after a coma, a stroke, and a period of depression and neglect, the first thing he said to me at the hospital was: “I made money with her.” He didn’t seem to care that my mother and I had lost each other for ever, before she could even get a break or any chance at recovery. One thing that still haunts me is the amount of abuse that I didn’t witness, but which my father admitted to in a diary I re-read last year, having locked it away in my attic since his death in 2002.
In January 2001, a few weeks after my mother died, he wrote: “I should be glad to have escaped death, divorce or jail for murder. I came close to killing Sally about six times … she insulted me.”
Shortly after, he wrote that he had started bringing other women to the house, telling one a “pack of lies” about my mother being “celibate” to get her into bed and writing graphically about having sex with her in the bed where my mother had been.
That same year, after his assault of a traffic warden in Brighton (which I believe is the only time he ever came close to being held accountable for the way he treated women), he stated in the diary: “Regret any mean act I did. Wish I had never done them.” He mentions being dressed down by my grandmother and some of my mother’s friends for how he had treated her. I have never heard from these friends and would like to.
Last year,, through an AncestryDNA test, I discovered who my mother’s father and grandfather were. Sally’s father – my grandfather – was Brian Hamnett from Rawdon in Yorkshire, an officer in the British navy during the second world war. Her grandfather was Ernest Hamnett from Manchester, an engineer for Mather & Platt with dozens of skills and certificates, and a Royal Engineer in the first world war. Like my mother, he was very artistic, having studied at Bradford school of art and the University of Manchester before moving across to the City of Leeds Training College in Headingley, where he was the “handwork” tutor, teaching every skill not done by machine.
At the time of my mother’s birth, Brian Hamnett was between marriages, but I know nothing concrete about his relationship with my grandmother. What I have discovered is that he had another daughter, a half-sister to Sally, living in London at the same time as her, who was a graphic designer and advertising art director. She died without ever knowing about my mother, but I have spoken to her friends and other family members and they say she would definitely have helped her.
I wish this was all I’d found out in the past few years, but in 2022 the American writer and feminist activist Letty Cottin Pogrebin claimed that Brian’s brother Brendan had tried to rape her in his room at the Chelsea Hotel in New York. This was in 1962, when she was a publicist for his US publisher. According to Shanda: A Memoir of Shame and Secrecy, Brendan threatened to smash a window in the hotel reception if he did not accompany her to his room, after which “he grabbed me, slammed the door behind us, and threw me on the bed … Suddenly I was on my back, and he was on top of me, thrusting, groping, stinking, sickening me with his sharp soured breath. I resisted with all the force I could muster.”
Pogrebin says she did not report the incident at the time, partly for fear of damaging her career. She now regrets that decision, although she is sure “Brendan would have retaliated with some scurrilous accusation that undoubtedly would have sullied my reputation more than his”. Her allegations have been ignored by most of the Irish media. In an email to me in 2024, Pogrebin described Brendan as a “devious devil who wore the cloak of an Irish charmer”.
But finding out about my mother’s family has given me the strength to break free from the Behans.
I can’t help wondering how Sally’s father and grandfather would have dealt with my father, and how different his behaviour might have been had they been around. Instead, he weaponised a focus on grand political causes and voiced support for IRA attacks, citing “700 years of rape and murder by the British”. I believe this was often a deflecting tactic to try to make my mother’s complaints seem trivial.
Also soul-destroying was the way in which his odious and inane views were showcased by various media outlets, including the Irish broadcaster RTÉ. In a televised interview from 1978, a clip of which is still online, he attacked the idea of the perfect mother as “nonsense”, explaining: “I think in many cases it gives rise to tremendous tensions within the family. I would imagine that most families strongly consider matricide.”
Meanwhile, in the Guardian in 1984, he got a chance to comment on the criminalisation of marital rape. “The possibilities of legal rape within marriage worry him,” the interviewer noted. “What sort of world will it be when a wife can change her mind after penetration, he wonders.”
In 1993 he was invited to appear on ITV’s Central Weekend Live from Birmingham and, having availed himself of the unlimited alcohol in the green room, spent the entire night after the appearance throwing my mother around his hotel room.
After the publication of a couple of successful books and plays, including Mother of All the Behans (1984) and Kathleen (1988), my father was placed on a pedestal by some parts of the British media. Yet instead of focusing on literary talent and original ideas, journalists developed a pattern of calling him for “entertaining” quotes and stories, including his habit of nude swimming in the sea off Brighton. There were frequent mentions of foreskins and “todgers”, and sexual references to politicians. Reading my father’s obituary in the Telegraph, I was disgusted to be reminded of his constant and frankly tedious claim to have founded the Male Liberation Front, and his quote: “Women drain you of your vital fluids, see. Men are suffering flak on an unprecedented scale; they need a divorced man like me to counsel them.”
Giving abusers attention like this not only encourages them, but makes it harder for victims to leave. It also, as we have seen with Russell Brand, creates armies of fans who, having been effectively told by the media that “this person is worthy of fame”, don’t ever want to see the other side. It’s all very well for certain titles now to look back and admit that, well, Brand wasn’t very funny after all, but had a certain kind of warped intelligence that was confused for eccentric transgression. Like many women, I always felt repulsed by Brand, could not understand his appeal and was alienated by the time and space given to him.
As with my father, leftwing ideologies served as a handy cloak, both shielding Brand from criticisms over his behaviour by most of the liberal media and allowing him outsize access to titles such as the Guardian, for which he penned more than 130 articles and blog posts, starting with sport but moving on to everything from politics to drug laws and addiction, obituaries and tributes, his views on the causes of social unrest and Margaret Thatcher and education policy. As the Guardian now admits on its website: “We recognise that his work with the Guardian contributed to Brand’s public profile … Some of the writing is vulgar, crass, graphic or misogynistic.”
I guess that’s something – but all this was obvious years ago. The Guardian and other outlets, notably the BBC and Channel 4, need to take a hard look not just at why Brand was platformed, but at why certain types of people are selected for media stardom despite their glaring flaws. This seems more cult than culture.
While a relatively small number of people knew for a fact what Brand (and my father) were doing behind closed doors, everyone who celebrated them knew of their repellent attitudes to women and laughed it off as some kind of joke, especially as they tended to pepper their sinister views with confusing comments in favour of feminism. Increasingly aware of the tragedy of her lost potential, my mother, for her part, told my father straight up that he was “boring” and a “cretin”.
The editors of the New Statesman, who had Brand guest edit a whole issue in October 2013, should perhaps have read Don Hennessy’s 2012 book How He Gets Into Her Head: The Mind of the Intimate Male Abuser, before literally portraying Brand as the Messiah. Hennessy talks about abuse and violence being driven by male entitlement to sexual priority over women and that at a very deep level, the abuser “wants to become God-like”.
Brand’s 10-and-a-half-year sentence still feels inadequate for all the damage he did, and his victims’ pain will continue after his release. We must soberly consider the wider opportunity cost that all the time, exposure and column inches devoted to Brand and other fringe narcissists have resulted in. Not only have the media alienated generations of women, but too many lives have been lost because we haven’t been told how to identify and avoid abusive relationships, or how to safely exit them.
Given the gender power imbalance that’s still so prevalent in our society and institutions, a “police and pick up the pieces” response is hardly going to work, and keeps the responsibility on the victims. While Brand may have been dealt with, more covert operators are carrying on as before. Officially, one in four adults over 16 will experience domestic violence, but when each case can involve thousands of individual offences and most people do not report, there are fewer issues that are more serious.
The platforming of abusive men also does a gross disservice to the real men, the quiet majority of non-abusers, whose positive contributions, voices, and ideas get pushed out by characters such as Brand, my father and so many others. It’s time for a real revolution, and that means shutting down this evil at the first available opportunity.
In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.
